newsitem.title: HUNGARY: TOP EUROPEON BANKER URGES RETAIL BANKING IN HUNGARY.
newsitem.headline: TOP EUROPEON BANKER URGES RETAIL BANKING IN HUNGARY.

text.p: The head of the European Monetary Institute told Hungarian bankers on Friday that while Hungary has made important steps towards an efficient banking system, much progress still has to be made in retail banking.
"The larger part of the Hungarian banking system is now in genuinely private hands," Alexandre Lamfalussy told a conference to mark the 10th anniversary of commercial banking in Hungary.

"The financial health of most banks...has improved, the legal, accounting and regulatory framework has been consolidated and...there is now an interbank payment system in place which can no longer be qualified as prehistoric."
However, he added more progress was necessary, especially in the in area retail and small business banking.
"In these fields, Hungarian banking is vastly underdeveloped," he said. "This is most regrettable... Households are and will remain the major source of the country's financial savings."
Lamfalussy added that there were also strong political reasons for developing retail services.
"Satisfied household and small enterprise customers provide you with the greatest public support," he said. "And I can assure you that you will need thias support in a democratic society."

Lamfalussy, reviewing Hungary's macroeconomic situation, said the country has improved in reducing the current account deficit to around $1.5 billion in 1996 from roughly $4 billion in 1994 and has reduced its external debt to around $13.3 billion at the end of last year from $18.9 billion at end-1994.
However, the majority of Hungarian paid a high price in lower standards of living, he added.
"Any further erosion of average living standards would be just as unsustainable as were the macroeconomic imbalances in 1993-94," he said.
"The standard of living should be allowed to begin to rise - but only to the extent that this does not upset the basic balance of the economy again."
Lamfalussy said Hungary's inflation is still high.
"The reduction of inflation must continue at a pace which puts the attainment of single-digit inflation in sight," he said.
Hungary reduced inflation to 23.5 percent last year from 28.2 percent in 1995, and targets some 17 percent for 1997 and 12 percent or even lower levels for 1998.
The EMI President also said that the country will have to begin to tackle earnestly the major structural problems related to the pension, health care, education and social security systems.
